newsitem.title: FINLAND: NIINISTO SEES MEAGRE 98 BUDGET TAX CUTS, MORE LATER.
newsitem.headline: NIINISTO SEES MEAGRE 98 BUDGET TAX CUTS, MORE LATER.

text.p: Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said on Thursday he would go for meagre income tax cuts in the government's state budget proposal for 1998.
"There is no reason to expect that the government would go beyond its tax targets," Niinisto told Reuters in an interview.
In the coalition coalition's August budget talks, Niinisto said he would propose "meagre but persuasive" income tax cuts. He gave no figures.
Government and parliament should be ready to take a new look at 1998 taxation in connection with pay talks next January, but not at the expense of the balance of state finances, he said.
This was not, however, a signal that the government wanted to "buy" an incomes settlement to its liking with new tax cuts, he said.
"The collective bargaining talks should be entirely between unions and employers who should agree on the right level of pay rises," Niinisto said.

"But technical preparations should be in place for us to take another look at 1998 taxation early in the year ... and of course it is in our interest that the incomes settlement is advantageous from the point of view of the national economy," he said.
"The unequivocal rule must be that any benefit (granted by the state) to anyone present (at the labour market negotiation table), will be paid by someone present," Niinisto added.
He was referring to this year's model under which the state aims to recover part of lost revenue from an income tax cut through higher energy taxation.

Political leaders have applauded the two-year nation-wide low-pay-rise settlement agreed in tripartite talks between the government, central trade unions and employer confederations in the autumn of 1995. That deal expires in February 1998.

The government has said modest pay rises together with income tax cuts lead to a better development of purchasing power than high nominal wage hikes, which raise labour costs and could trigger inflation.
The government programme agreed when the five-party cabinet took office in April 1995 says income taxes will be cut gradually throughout the four-year term to 1999.
Niinisto said there was no room for massive tax cuts.
The 1997 state budget is built around a 3.9 percent growth forecast which should lead to a fall in the unemployment rate to 15.4 percent from on average 16.3 percent in 1996.
The budget deficit is projected at 28 billion markka, down from 34 billion last year.
"These are quite optimistic numbers and they must come true for us (the budget deficit) to be on track. It is unfounded to think we would be able to do very much better," Niinisto said.
Even if unemployment were zero and the state paid no jobless benefits the budget would remain in deficit, he said.
Finland will face in coming years strong pressures from the EU to harmonise taxation, mainly excise duties, with EU norms.
Such steps would create big gaps in Finnish state revenue. It was of "utmost importance" to try to bring the state finances close to balance, preferably into surplus, Niinisto said.
He repeated the government's pledge to not finance any 1997 supplementary budget by increased net borrowing.

Niinisto also said he hoped privatisations of state-owned companies could bring in "something else" than the one billion markka revenue targetted in the 1997 state budget. He did not elaborate. -- Helsinki Newsroom +358 - 9 - 680 50 245
